objectives: Reason about DRC, LVS, and tape-out gates.

slides.title: ASIC vs FPGA + the design hierarchy
slides.body:
**ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit)**: custom chip fabricated for a specific design. Once fabricated, can't change.

**Trade-offs vs FPGA**:
- ✅ ~10× faster, more power-efficient, smaller area.
- ✅ Cheaper per unit at high volumes.
- ❌ Massive NRE: \$10-100M for advanced nodes.
- ❌ Tape-out turnaround: 3-9 months.
- ❌ Can't be changed once fabricated.

**Design hierarchy**:
- **Cell**: smallest unit. NAND, NOR, FF, MUX (from standard-cell library).
- **Block**: a few thousand gates implementing a functional unit (ALU, register file).
- **Module**: thousands-millions of gates (a CPU core, a memory controller).
- **Chip / SoC**: entire silicon die. Modern: 10+ billion transistors.

**Modern process nodes**:
- 28 nm: cheap, mature. Used for low-cost products.
- 16/14 nm: previous gen, still widely used.
- 7 nm: TSMC, current high-end.
- 5 nm: Apple M-series, NVIDIA H100.
- 3 nm: Apple A17, M3.
- 2 nm (coming 2025): Intel + TSMC roadmap.

Each node ~30% smaller + ~25% faster than previous. Node costs grow exponentially: 7nm tape-out ~\$10M; 3nm ~\$80M+.

**Standard-cell libraries**: pre-designed cells (NAND2_X1, FF, AOI22 etc.) characterized for timing/power/area at each process node. Provided by the foundry or third parties (Arm Artisan). Modern libraries have ~1000-5000 cells of varying drive strengths.

**IP blocks**: pre-designed modules (USB, PCIe, DDR, ARM cores). Licensed for ~\$M each. SoCs are mostly licensed IP + a few proprietary blocks.

**The team**: front-end designers (RTL + verification), back-end designers (synthesis, P&R, timing), DV (design verification, ~50-70% of headcount in modern projects), physical design, test, layout. Modern advanced-node tape-outs employ hundreds-thousands of engineers + take years.

slides.title: RTL-to-GDSII flow
slides.body:
**GDSII (or OASIS)**: the geometric file format submitted to the foundry. Describes layout polygons per layer.

The 12-stage flow from RTL → GDSII:

1. **RTL design** (Verilog/SystemVerilog).
2. **Functional verification**: simulation, formal verification, emulation (Veloce, Palladium, Zebu, Protium).
3. **Synthesis**: RTL → technology-mapped gate netlist. Tools: Synopsys Design Compiler, Cadence Genus.
4. **Equivalence checking**: prove synthesized netlist matches RTL. Tools: Synopsys Formality, Cadence Conformal.
5. **Floorplanning**: lay out major blocks on chip; place macros (memories, IP); plan power grid.
6. **Placement**: assign each cell a location. Tools: Synopsys IC Compiler, Cadence Innovus.
7. **Clock-tree synthesis (CTS)**: build clock distribution network to minimize skew.
8. **Routing**: connect all cells via metal layers. Modern designs have 10-20 metal layers.
9. **Static Timing Analysis (STA)**: verify timing closure across all corners (process / voltage / temperature combinations).
10. **DRC (Design Rule Check)**: verify layout meets foundry geometric rules (spacing, widths, density).
11. **LVS (Layout vs Schematic)**: verify layout's connectivity matches the synthesized netlist.
12. **GDSII tape-out + manufacturing handoff**.

**Tool suites** ('Big 3 EDA'): Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens (formerly Mentor). Each owns multi-million-dollar tools. License fees ~\$1M/seat/year for advanced flows.

**Open-source alternatives**: Yosys (synthesis), OpenROAD (P&R), Magic / KLayout (layout). Used by Google's MPW (Multi-Project Wafer) initiatives (Caravel, OpenLane). Free 130 nm + 90 nm tape-outs available for educational use.

**Closure metrics**:
- **Timing closure**: 0 violations in STA.
- **DRC clean**: 0 DRC errors.
- **LVS clean**: 0 LVS errors.
- **Power closure**: meets target power.
- **Area closure**: meets die-size budget.

All must be closed simultaneously before tape-out.

slides.title: Verification + the 70% rule
slides.body:
**Verification consumes ~50-70% of an ASIC project's effort**. Why: a bug discovered after tape-out costs ~\$10-50M (re-spin: months of delay + new mask set).

**Verification methodology**:

**Directed tests**: hand-written testbenches covering specific scenarios. Necessary but insufficient.

**Constrained random**: generate random stimuli with constraints (e.g., 'random valid Ethernet packets'). Discovers corner cases.

**UVM (Universal Verification Methodology)**: SystemVerilog framework for constrained-random verification. Industry standard. Components: agents, drivers, monitors, scoreboards, sequences.

**Functional coverage**: track which scenarios have been hit. 'Did we test packet sizes 1, 64, 1500, 9000?' 'Did we test all FSM transitions?' Coverage drives test development.

**Code coverage**: which RTL lines / branches were executed. Useful but doesn't catch missed cases.

**Formal verification**: prove properties mathematically (no random inputs needed). Used for safety-critical logic (cache coherence, security units). Tools: Jasper, OneSpin.

**Emulation**: run RTL on a custom emulator (Veloce Strato, Palladium Z2) at ~1-10 MHz. Run OS boot, full software stacks. Hours-to-days per scenario vs years on simulation.

**Prototyping**: synthesize RTL to large FPGAs (Cadence Protium, S2C Prodigy). Even faster than emulation; closer to silicon behavior.

**Silicon validation**: post-fab, real chip tested. Last chance to catch issues.

**Bug examples**:
- **FDIV bug (Pentium 1994)**: floating-point divider gave wrong results. Recall cost Intel \$475M.
- **Spectre/Meltdown (2018)**: speculation-leak bugs across architectures.
- **AMD Zen 4 BIOS bug (2023)**: certain Asus boards killed CPUs. Hardware + microcode interaction.

Verification quality determines whether silicon works. 'It's working in simulation' doesn't mean working post-fab. Decades of methodology have been built to bridge the gap.

question.question: Compute area + cost for a die at different nodes
question.goal: A design needs 100 million transistors. Compare implementation at 28nm vs 7nm. Transistor density: 28nm ~3 MT/mm², 7nm ~96 MT/mm². Wafer cost: 28nm ~\$2K/wafer, 7nm ~\$17K/wafer.

steps.prompt: Cost per die: wafer cost / dies-per-wafer. 300mm wafer ≈ 70,000 mm². At 28nm: ~70000/33 ≈ 2100 dies, so cost/die = \$2000/2100 ≈ \$1. At 7nm: ~70000 dies/wafer, cost/die ≈ \$0.24. Lower per-die cost at smaller node!

options: 7nm CHEAPER per die — denser packing offsets higher wafer cost. Plus performance + power advantages.

steps.reveal: 7nm is cheaper per die DESPITE higher wafer cost — because density gain (32×) exceeds wafer-cost gain (8.5×). The catch: NRE is much higher at 7nm (\$10-50M vs \$5M at 28nm). 7nm pays off only at volume.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Cost = NRE + (wafer cost / dies per wafer) × volume}}$$ Modern node decisions: at high volume (smartphones, data center), advanced nodes pay off via per-die cost + performance. At low volume, mature nodes (28nm, 16nm) are cheaper total. Foundries (TSMC, Samsung, Intel Foundry Services) charge by wafer; designers shop nodes based on volume + performance needs. Apple, NVIDIA, Qualcomm always at leading edge; automotive + medical often at 28nm/40nm (mature, well-characterized).

question.question: An ASIC tape-out at 7nm costs ~\$15M in NRE + masks. A bug is discovered post-fab. Why is a 're-spin' so expensive?
options: Engineers are paid by the bug.
Requires re-doing one or more mask layers (~\$2-5M for advanced nodes), several months delay, lost market window, possibly customer penalties + product-recall costs.
question.explanation: Re-spin: new mask set (1-20+ layers, depending on bug scope), fabrication delay (3-6 months at 7nm), opportunity cost (competitors ship while you're stuck). Total: \$5-15M direct + huge indirect costs. Hence the verification investment. Companies have shipped projects with known bugs + worked around them in software/microcode rather than re-spin.

hints: What else does a re-spin cost?
slides.workedSolution: 7nm mask set: ~\$15M+. A re-spin = redo affected masks (often \$5M+ even for partial fix) + 3-6 months delay + lost market window. Plus customer dissatisfaction. Hence verification is 50-70% of effort. When bugs are found post-fab, common workarounds: microcode patches (Intel), driver software fixes, marketing the feature as 'experimental'. Re-spin is the last resort.

question.question: Apple A17 Pro: 19 billion transistors in 103 mm² at 3nm. Density (MT/mm²)?
Pipeline-rebalancing for timing closure
question.prompt: A chip targets 3 GHz but synthesis reports max 2.5 GHz. The synthesis tool flags a critical path through a 32-bit divider. Walk through how you would close timing.
Explain in two or three sentences why ASIC design verification consumes 50-70% of the project effort.
question.rubric: Mentions that post-fab bugs cost \$5-50M (re-spin), with months of delay; testing every input combination is impossible; verification methodology (UVM, formal, emulation, coverage) systematically explores the design space; even with all this, advanced chips ship with errata documents listing known bugs. Compared to software (cheap to patch), hardware bugs are existential — hence the investment.
